records.summary: 2989 24th St sits in the NCT-24TH-MISSION zoning district where a Restaurant serving beer and wine is a conditional use; the property also falls within the Mission Alcoholic Beverage Special Use District, which permits restaurants operating as bona fide eating places to serve alcohol, and the Calle 24 Special Use District, which may restrict new restaurants if they would push restaurant/bar frontage over 35% within 300 feet (the records do not show that share). The site currently has an active Type 21 off-sale general liquor license (a corner store or market) that has been in place since 1981. Within 500 feet there are 6 active on-sale ABC licenses and 11 registered food/drink businesses, signaling a dense commercial corridor; 27 on-sale licenses exist within 1,000 feet, raising an undue-concentration flag. Over the last 10 years only 5 dated use decisions were filed within 1,000 feet in this district—too few to compute an approval rate—but 3 of those were approved (1 outright, 2 with conditions) and 2 were withdrawn; no restaurant or bar CUA in that window was denied.

patterns.pattern: Restaurant conditional use authorizations in the NCT-24th-Mission district on the 24th Street corridor between Mission and Alabama were uniformly approved over the last 35 years; the records show no denials of restaurant CUAs in this immediate area, and timelines for decided cases ranged from 2 to 13 months depending on scope (new use vs. ownership change vs. alcohol addition).

When beer-and-wine service was added to an existing restaurant via CUA, the Commission imposed hours-of-operation limits (6 AM to 2 AM in the one case with extracted conditions) and standard eating-and-drinking conditions: sidewalk maintenance within a one-block radius, soundproofing, odor control equipment, waste management, and appointment of a community liaison officer.

Planning Department ABC referrals (Type 41, beer and wine for eating places) in the NCT-24th-Mission district and Mission Alcoholic Beverage SUD were approved as a matter of course when the applicant operated as a bona fide eating place and met Planning Code Section 202.2(a) conditions; these referrals do not predict conditional-use hearing outcomes but show Planning's baseline support for beer-a…

Change-of-use applications from retail or limited restaurant to full-service restaurant in the immediate vicinity (within 100 meters) were approved in 2–4.5 months when no alcohol was initially involved, and in 13 months when beer-and-wine service was added, suggesting alcohol additions trigger longer environmental and neighborhood-notice timelines.

The addresses immediately adjacent to 2989 24th St (2980–2990 24th St, 43 m away) have held continuous restaurant approvals since 1990 and currently operate with an active Type 41 ABC license, demonstrating the Commission views this block as an established restaurant corridor compatible with on-sale beer-and-wine service.

The Mission Alcoholic Beverage Special Use District permits restaurants to serve alcohol when operated as bona fide eating places, and all restaurant CUAs in the district since 2011 that disclosed the SUD in their description were approved, indicating the SUD does not function as a prohibition on restaurant alcohol service but rather channels it through conditional use review.

denial_signals: No denials found among the ten comparable cases; the records show two withdrawn CUAs within 1,000 feet over the last decade (outside the immediate corridor) but neither record states a reason for withdrawal

findings.text: Zoning district NCT-24th-Mission requires conditional use for a restaurant on the first story per Planning Code § 763, in force since January 2024.

Mission Alcoholic Beverage Special Use District requires conditional use for any restaurant in the sub-area east of the Mission Street NCT and north of Cesar Chavez; the NCT-24th-Mission district lies inside that sub-area per Planning Code § 249.60(f)(1).

Calle 24 Special Use District prohibits a new restaurant where restaurants, limited restaurants and bars take up, or would with the project take up, more than 35% of commercial frontage (linear feet) within 300 feet of the site; the records do not show that share of frontage per Planning Code § 249.59(d)(1).

Nine restaurant conditional use authorizations on the 24th Street corridor between Alabama and Mission (within 130 meters) were approved over the last 35 years, including 2956 24th St (57 m, 2019), 2962 24th St (51 m, 2011), 2980 24th St (43 m, 2001 and 1990), 2965 24th St (41 m, 1997) and 2969–2973 24th St (28 m, 2003); no restaurant CUA in this area was denied.

The directly adjacent property at 2990 24th St (43 m) has held continuous restaurant approvals since 1990 and operates with an active Type 41 ABC license as of 2022, demonstrating Commission acceptance of restaurant use next door.

Among comparable restaurant CUAs with extracted conditions, the Commission imposed hours limited to 6 AM–2 AM daily, standard eating-and-drinking conditions (sidewalk maintenance within one block, soundproofing, odor control, waste management) and appointment of a community liaison officer at 2956 24th St in 2019.

findings.text: Census tract 229.02 holds 10 active on-sale retail licenses against 7 authorized per ABC's census tract authorizations of September 2026, so the tract is over its authorized number and state law tests a new license and a transfer from other premises for undue concentration per California Business and Professions Code § 23958.4.

Mission Alcoholic Beverage Special Use District permits a restaurant operating as a bona fide eating place to serve alcohol; its license may be transferred from inside or from outside the district, and the district adds no conditional use for the license itself per Planning Code § 249.60(b)(1)(A).

ABC referrals for Type 41 licenses (beer and wine, eating place) in the NCT-24th-Mission district were approved by Planning when the applicant operated as a bona fide eating place and met Planning Code § 202.2(a) conditions; examples include 2817 24th St (March 2023) and 2962 24th St (November 2017).
An active Type 21 off-sale general liquor license (corner store or market) has been on file at 2989 24th St since November 1981, indicating the current use is retail alcohol sales, not a restaurant.

Within 500 feet there are 6 active on-sale ABC licenses (four Type 41, one Type 20, one Type 48) and 27 on-sale licenses within 1,000 feet, signaling a dense alcohol corridor and triggering an undue-concentration flag.

approvals.summary: A restaurant with full cooking needs a health permit to operate, issued after plan check and inspection without a hearing; DPH plan check for a new restaurant in this district is a flat fee of $2,207 (8 hours) as of FY 2026–27, and the permit application is $470.

findings.text: A food business needs a health permit to operate, issued by SF Department of Public Health after plan check and final inspection confirm the facility matches approved plans and a certified food safety manager is on staff, per California Retail Food Code §§ 114380–114381 and SF Health Code Article 8.

DPH plan check for a new restaurant (full kitchen, tenant improvements) is a flat fee of $2,207 for 8 hours of review as of FY 2026–27, with extra review at $276/hour, and requires approval of plans, finishes, equipment and menu per the catalog entry.
The FY 2026–27 health permit application fee is $470 (includes initial inspection) and the annual license fee for restaurants and bars is $0 for 2026–28; reinspections are $276/hour.

The description states tenant improvements and full cooking are planned, which trigger a building permit with kitchen build-out, hood, restrooms, ADA upgrades and plans stamped by an architect per the catalog entry.

Building Code classifies a restaurant or bar as Assembly Group A-2, and a space for fewer than 50 people as Group B per 2022 California Building Code § 303.1.1 and § 303.3; the description does not give whether the space is for fewer than 50 people, so the proposed occupancy group is not established.
The existing occupancy group of the space is not in public records; only plans or an inspection show it, so a change of occupancy is not established.

expected_conditions.condition: Hours of operation limited to 6:00 AM to 2:00 AM daily, with no service after 2:00 AM.
expected_conditions.basis: The most recent restaurant CUA with beer-and-wine service in this district (2956 24th St, 57 m away, decided November 2019) imposed hours of 6 AM to 2 AM Monday through Sunday. State law prohibits on-sale alcohol service after 2 AM, and the Commission typically conditions restaurant alcohol approvals in neighborhood commercial districts to end service at 2 AM.

expected_conditions.condition: Operate as a bona fide eating place where food service is the principal business and alcohol sales are incidental to meals, per California Business and Professions Code § 23038 and Planning Code § 249.60(b)(1)(A).
expected_conditions.basis: Mission Alcoholic Beverage Special Use District permits restaurants to serve alcohol only when operated as bona fide eating places; ABC referrals in this district uniformly require this condition, and Planning Code § 249.60(b)(1)(A) states it explicitly.

expected_conditions.condition: Comply with Planning Code § 202.2(a) operating conditions: maintain a good-neighbor policy, respond to complaints, control noise and litter, and post the policy on-site.
expected_conditions.basis: Planning Code § 249.60(d) requires all liquor establishments in the Mission Alcoholic Beverage SUD to comply with § 202.2 operating conditions, and ABC referrals for restaurants in this district cite § 202.2(a) as a condition.

expected_conditions.condition: Provide exterior lighting, keep window signage to 33% of window area, and maintain 50% clear glazing on street-facing facades.
expected_conditions.basis: Planning Code § 249.60(d) requires new, relocated or expanded liquor establishments in the Mission Alcoholic Beverage SUD (and any with a license referred to Planning by ABC) to provide outside lighting, limit window signage to 33%, and keep 50% clear glazing on street-facing facades.

expected_conditions.condition: Maintain the main entrance and all sidewalks abutting the property in a clean and sanitary condition, and monitor the sidewalk within a one-block radius daily during business hours to keep it free of litter associated with the business.
expected_conditions.basis: The 2019 CUA for a restaurant with beer and wine at 2956 24th St (57 m away) imposed this condition, citing Department of Public Works Street and Sidewalk Maintenance Standards and SF Police Code Article 1, § 34. This is a standard eating-and-drinking condition in neighborhood commercial districts.

expected_conditions.condition: Adequately soundproof or insulate the premises so that incidental noise is not audible beyond the premises or in other sections of the building, and ensure fixed-source equipment noise does not exceed the decibel levels in the SF Noise Control Ordinance.
expected_conditions.basis: Standard eating-and-drinking condition imposed at 2956 24th St (57 m, 2019) to protect nearby residents from restaurant noise, particularly in mixed-use buildings with residential units above commercial spaces.

expected_conditions.condition: Install and maintain appropriate odor control equipment in conformance with approved plans to prevent any significant noxious or offensive odors from escaping the premises.
expected_conditions.basis: Standard condition imposed at 2956 24th St (57 m, 2019) for restaurants with full cooking; DPH plan check and building permit review typically require hood and odor control equipment details on the plans.

expected_conditions.condition: Keep garbage, recycling and compost containers within the premises and hidden from public view, and place them outside only when being serviced by the disposal company.
expected_conditions.basis: Standard eating-and-drinking condition for waste management imposed at 2956 24th St (57 m, 2019), citing Department of Public Works garbage and recycling receptacles guidelines.

expected_conditions.condition: Appoint a community liaison officer to deal with issues of concern to owners and occupants of nearby properties, and provide the Zoning Administrator and all registered neighborhood groups with written notice of the liaison's name, business address and telephone number.
expected_conditions.basis: Standard condition imposed at 2956 24th St (57 m, 2019) prior to issuance of a building permit, to ensure ongoing communication with the neighborhood during construction and operation.

filing_playbook.action: Confirm with Planning Department whether restaurant/bar frontage within 300 feet of 2989 24th St exceeds 35% under Calle 24 SUD § 249.59(d)(1).
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Submit a zoning inquiry to the Planning Information Center (628-652-7300 or pic@sfgov.org) or request a pre-application meeting, stating the address (2989 24th St, parcel 4270/033) and asking: 'Does the proposed restaurant use comply with Calle 24 Special Use District Planning Code § 249.59(d)(1)? Specifically, what percentage of commercial frontage within 300 feet of the site is occupied by restaurants, limited restaurants and bars, and would the project push that share over 35%?' If Planning confirms the share is under 35% or the site is exempt, proceed to file the CUA. If over 35%, the project is not permitted as described and the concept must be revised or the site abandoned.

filing_playbook.action: File conditional use authorization application with SF Planning Department for a restaurant use under Planning Code § 303.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Submit the CUA application online via Planning's permit portal. State that the project is a change of use from retail (off-sale alcohol, Type 21 license holder since 1981) to a restaurant with full kitchen and beer-and-wine service (ABC Type 41). Describe the concept as a bona fide eating place where food is the principal business and alcohol is incidental to meals. Declare whether the business is part of a chain (formula retail) and provide the floor area in square feet. State that the restaurant will close by 2 AM and will not offer entertainment. Note that the project is in the NCT-24th-Mission district, the Mission Alcoholic Beverage Special Use District and the Calle 24 Special Use District, and that Planning confirmed (in step 1) compliance with the Calle 24 35% frontage rule. Attach a pre-application community meeting summary showing outreach to registered neighborhood groups wit…

filing_playbook.action: Respond to Planning Department environmental review and neighborhood notification (Section 311 posted notice for 30 days).
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Planning will route the CUA for environmental review under CEQA and post a Section 311 notice at the site for 30 days, mailing notice to property owners and registered neighborhood groups within 300 feet. Monitor for any discretionary review requests or appeals filed during the notice period. If a discretionary review request is filed, Planning will schedule it for a hearing; address the concerns raised in the DR request in writing and at the hearing.

filing_playbook.action: Attend Planning Commission hearing and respond to any conditions or continuances.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Prepare a presentation (5–10 minutes) describing the restaurant concept, the neighborhood fit (cite the nine approved restaurant CUAs within 130 meters over 35 years, including the directly adjacent property at 2990 24th St with an active Type 41 license), the operating plan (hours 6 AM to 2 AM, bona fide eating place, full kitchen, no entertainment), and how the project will meet Mission Alcoholic Beverage SUD requirements (§ 202.2 good-neighbor policy, exterior lighting, 33% window signage limit, 50% clear glazing). Commit to the standard eating-and-drinking conditions: sidewalk maintenance within one block, soundproofing, odor control, waste management, and appointment of a community liaison. Bring an architect or expediter who has presented to the Commission. If the Commission continues the hearing to request more information (neighborhood outreach, design changes, operating plan de…

filing_playbook.action: After CUA approval, file building permit application with DBI for tenant improvements and change of use, routing it to Planning, DPH and Fire.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Submit the building permit application online via SF-DBI's permit portal with plans stamped by a licensed architect showing the kitchen layout, hood and fire suppression system, restrooms, ADA upgrades, finishes and equipment. State on the application that the use is a restaurant approved by Planning Commission under CUA case number [insert case number from step 4] and that the plans implement the conditions of approval in the Commission's motion. Ensure the application is routed to Planning (for zoning sign-off), DPH Environmental Health (for plan check) and Fire (for hood and place-of-assembly review if occupant load is 50 or more). The architect or expediter should coordinate plan check comments from all three departments and submit revised plans until approval.

filing_playbook.action: Submit DPH plan check for new food facility in parallel with or immediately after the building permit application.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Apply online through DPH's Environmental Health portal with two sets of scaled drawings, interior/exterior photos, and a menu describing preparation methods. State that the facility is a new restaurant with full cooking and request the new-restaurant plan check (8 hours, $2,207 flat fee as of FY 2026–27). The plans must show the three-compartment sink, hand sinks, hot water, finishes, equipment, food storage, waste disposal and the location of the grease interceptor. After DPH approves the plans, schedule a pre-final inspection at approximately 80% construction complete and a final inspection before opening, booking each with the plan reviewer at least two weeks in advance.

filing_playbook.action: Apply for health permit to operate after final DPH inspection and once a certified food safety manager is on staff.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Submit the health permit application online at least one month before the planned opening date, paying the $470 permit application fee (FY 2026–27). Provide proof that at least one owner or employee has passed an ANSI-accredited food safety certification exam within 60 days of opening. DPH will issue the permit after the final inspection confirms the facility matches the approved plans and the certified manager is on staff.

filing_playbook.action: Apply to ABC for a Type 41 license after Planning's CUA approval, and submit Planning's CUA approval letter and DPH health permit when ABC requests the zoning sign-off.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: File the ABC Type 41 application online at ABC's eFiling portal with the signed lease, seller's permit, entity registration, and the $1,000 application fee. Describe the business as a bona fide eating place where food service is the principal business and alcohol is incidental to meals. ABC will mail a 30-day posting notice; post it at the premises in a front window visible from the street for 30 days and photograph it weekly. ABC will refer the application to SFPD and SF Planning for review. When Planning requests documents, submit the Planning Commission's CUA approval motion and the DPH health permit. If the census tract is over its authorized number (which it is: 10 active on-sale licenses against 7 authorized), ABC may require a Public Convenience or Necessity letter from the city; start that process when ABC notifies you, working with Planning and the District Supervisor's office.…

timeline_cost.notes: Timeline is 120–300 days from CUA filing to approval for the conditional use authorization and health permit, the two approvals in the entitlement path given by the rules. Comparable restaurant CUAs with beer-and-wine service in this district took 28 days (a 2003 self-service restaurant across the street), 126 days (a 2011 full-service restaurant 51 m away), 133 days (a 2001 full-service restaurant next door at 43 m), and 408 days (a 2018 change from restaurant to restaurant with beer and wine at 57 m). The 408-day case is an outlier reflecting a more complex environmental review or continuances; typical timelines are 4–6 months when the application is complete and neighborhood outreach is documented. Cost is $3,100–$6,700 in government fees for the CUA (base fee approximately $3,100–$3,150 as of 2025, not in the catalog), health plan check ($2,207 for new restaurant, 8 hours) and health permit ($470). These figures are for the time and cost to obtain the two approvals when they are granted; they are not a time to a denial or a withdrawal. The building permit and ABC license are in insufficient-information status (the building permit because change of use and change of occupancy are not established, the ABC license because how the license will be obtained is not given), so their time and cost are not included here. If the Calle 24 SUD 35% frontage rule prohibits the project, there is no approval path and no timeline or cost applies.
